extracted.intended_audience: systematic reviewers, meta-analysts, health technology assessors and research methodologists
extracted.subtask_short: assessing publication bias in systematic reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for identifying, testing for, and judging publication and related dissemination biases in systematic reviews and meta-analyses of health research. Includes what to search, which tests to use, and how to rate review authors' efforts and risk of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of review type
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify systematic reviews into categories: (1) studies on effects of health-care interventions, (2) studies on accuracy of diagnostic tests, (3) epidemiological studies on association between risk factors and health outcomes, and (4) genetic studies on association between genes and disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different review types may face different dissemination/publishing bias patterns and should be assessed separately (the review sampled reviews from MEDLINE and classified them into these categories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative review vs meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish reviews that summarise primary studies without statistical combination (narrative systematic reviews) from those that use statistical methods to combine results of two or more primary studies (meta-analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication and related biases are more often dealt with in meta-analyses than in narrative reviews; expect greater use of formal tests (e.g., funnel plots) in meta-analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of literature search (databases and sources searched)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which bibliographic databases and other sources were searched (examples listed: MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, specialized databases like LILACS and SIGLE, checking references, handsearching, contacting authors/experts, companies, conference proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough literature search may reduce excluding unpublished studies, non-English-language studies or grey literature. It is advisable to search more than one electronic database because many journals are indexed in only one commonly used database.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching prospective trial registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether prospective registers of clinical trials and other studies were searched for unpublished or ongoing studies (examples: UK National Research Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, Physician Data Query register, Current Controlled Trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching trial registers is a common method to identify unpublished or ongoing studies and helps reduce publication bias; report which registers were searched and how many reviews searched them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language restriction reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether review authors applied language restrictions (e.g. restricted to English only), whether they explicitly stated 'no language restriction', or whether language restriction was unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report explicitly if language restrictions were applied. Searching for non-English-language studies and including them can reduce language bias. The extent of searching for non-English studies varies (from no restriction in a search to targeted searches in non-English databases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching for and including non-English-language studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether non-English-language studies were explicitly searched for and whether non-English-language studies were actually included in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly searching for non-English-language studies was reported in an increasing proportion of reviews; however, explicit search does not always equate to inclusion. Indicate whether non-English studies were searched for or included and how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grey literature and unpublished studies search
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether grey literature (defined as outputs not controlled by commercial publishers) and other unpublished studies were sought (common methods: searching conference abstracts, meeting proceedings, grey literature databases like SIGLE and LILACS, contacting authors/experts and companies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly seeking grey literature/unpublished studies reduces risk of publication bias; report whether grey literature was searched for and whether it was included. Different review types vary in how often grey literature is sought/included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of outcome reporting bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether outcome reporting bias (selective reporting of some measured outcomes within published studies) was explicitly considered or reported in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome reporting bias is distinct from publication bias but related; indicate if the review examined outcome reporting bias, reported missing outcome data, or used protocol versus report comparisons. This was explicitly mentioned in a minority of reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods used to detect/test for publication bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Which statistical or other methods were used to test for publication bias (examples listed: funnel plot and related methods, Egger's test, Begg's test, trim-and-fill method, fail-safe N, modelling, identifying unpublished trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funnel plots often complemented by Egger's and Begg's tests are common in meta-analyses; some methods (fail-safe N) have become less used. Report which methods were used and the results (evidence for/against publication bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion/consideration of publication bias in the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the possibility of publication bias was discussed or mentioned in the review and whether authors interpreted results with caution when publication bias was considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication bias was discussed more often in meta-analyses than narrative reviews. When publication bias is discussed, authors more often interpret results cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efforts taken to minimise publication bias — sufficiency categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgement categories for efforts taken to minimise publication bias: 'sufficient' if review attempted to search and probably include non-English-language studies, grey literature and unpublished studies, considered outcome reporting bias and publication bias, and reported any missing outcome data; 'partial' if at least two of the three searches (non-English, grey literature, unpublished) were done and may or may not have considered outcome reporting or publication bias; 'insufficient' if no attempts were made to search non-English, grey or unpublished studies, and neither outcome reporting bias nor publication bias nor missing outcome data were reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors used these definitions to rate each review. These judgements were converted to numeric scores: insufficient = 0; partial = 1; sufficient = 2. Use the same component checklist when assigning categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring conversion for minimisation-effort assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric conversion of the sufficiency judgements for pooling and analysis: insufficient = 0; partial = 1; sufficient = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert assessor judgements into these scores and pool across assessors as needed for summary statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of risk of publication bias — low/moderate/high definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk of bias judged as 'high' if efforts to minimise publication bias were partial or insufficient, publication bias was not discussed and the authors' conclusions were positive; 'moderate' if partial efforts were taken, publication bias was probably considered, and the authors' conclusions might have been positive with cautious interpretation; 'low' if partial or sufficient efforts were taken, publication bias was considered with some methods used to deal with it, and the authors' conclusions were negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are qualitative criteria for perceived risk and were converted to scores: low = 0, moderate = 1, high = 2. Use the combined evidence from search efforts, discussion, methods used, and conclusions to assign risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring conversion for risk-of-bias assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Numeric conversion of perceived risk categories for analysis: low = 0; moderate = 1; high = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these numeric codes when aggregating assessors' judgements across reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment procedure and inter-assessor process
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of two independent assessors to evaluate each review with disagreements resolved by discussion or a third reviewer; reporting of inter-rater agreement statistics (κ) and agreement rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent duplicate assessment increases reliability; report kappa statistics and percent agreement for different review types. Note that many variables were assessed subjectively as 'yes', 'no' or 'unclear', which can lose information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of authors' conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify review authors' conclusions as 'positive', 'not positive' or 'unclear' and use this classification when analysing associations with publication bias and risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors' conclusions were examined in relation to whether publication bias was tested or considered; e.g., positive conclusions proportions varied by review type. Use this classification as an input to risk assessment (positive conclusions with insufficient efforts increases perceived risk).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and explicit reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should explicitly report sources searched, language restrictions, whether non-English or grey/unpublished studies were searched for and included, outcome reporting considerations, methods used to detect publication bias, and any missing outcome data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of clear reporting (e.g., 'unclear' whether non-English studies were searched) hampers assessment of risk and efforts. Explicit reporting of search strategy components is a quality indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of statistical tests selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose and report appropriate statistical methods to detect publication bias (use funnel plot plus complementary tests like Egger's and Begg's when data allow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funnel plots and related methods are commonly used; some methods (e.g., fail-safe N) have declined in use. Rarely used methods (trim-and-fill, modelling, identifying unpublished trials) may still be informative but should be applied and interpreted cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider heterogeneity and review context when interpreting publication-bias tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for heterogeneity among included studies, differences in study designs and other characteristics when interpreting tests for publication bias and when generalising findings from empirical studies of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large cohort empirical studies are diverse; confounding factors (sample size, design, research question) may influence both results and likelihood of publication. Interpretation of publication-bias tests should consider these limitations.
